A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and the equations, experiments, and figures can be matched despite renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original CLEVR and SDXL generation experiments, including length-generalization and color composition, plus synthetic sampling experiments in the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds quantitative CLEVR counts and an original analysis of CLIP image and text embeddings.

M1.justification: Section 8.2 adds an auxiliary diagnostic that compares background-centered CLIP concept embeddings to predict composition compatibility, using either representative images or text prompts. The existing composition operator, diffusion architectures, and sampling procedures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Figure 8 and Appendix D add a representative-image and text-prompt collection covering seven animal, style, and accessory concepts plus a background. Existing generative tasks remain unchanged; Table 1's N=1–6 CLEVR evaluation falls within the previously tested length-generalization coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 evaluates the same empty-background, single-object Bayes, and cluttered Bayes constructions already compared in Figure 3. The existing synthetic DDIM and Langevin comparisons are retained, without an added baseline.

E3.justification: Beyond v1's visual CLEVR assessment, Table 1 introduces a stated 100-sample protocol with manual counts of correctly located objects for N=1–6. The new CLIP experiment introduces filtered image collections and cosine comparisons of background-centered image and text embeddings. These substantially expand evaluation procedures; existing training and sampling settings are retained.

E4.justification: The background-choice analysis gains quantitative object-placement histograms in Table 1. Figure 8 adds an exploratory analysis of concept-group orthogonality using image and text embeddings. Earlier color-composition, clutter, and nonorthogonal-sampling analyses remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new CLEVR histograms describe generated samples, rather than estimating uncertainty, and the CLIP averages serve as diagnostic inputs.

E6.justification: v2 adds quantitative CLEVR results and CLIP similarity heatmaps. At N=6, Table 1 reports six correctly located objects in 97 empty-background and 98 cluttered-Bayes samples out of 100. These are newly reported results, not performance gains over v1. The Single-object Bayes rows for N=2 and N=6 total 109 and 43, contradicting the stated sample count.

T1.justification: Adds Lemma 8.1 and its proof that factorized conditionals imply orthogonal mean differences. Appendix J is substantially revised as Appendix K: mixture-weight normalization is corrected, two-sided Wasserstein bounds are developed, and new Lemma K.9 establishes a constant discrepancy between composition and Gaussian noising. A further bound describes how this discrepancy decreases for large tau.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution summary add a practical heuristic for predicting whether new compositions will succeed. The central claims concerning projective composition, length-generalization, factorized conditionals, and sampling guarantees and failures are retained.

C2.justification: Section 8.2 interprets CLIP concept-group separation as a possible indicator of composability, explicitly qualifying mean orthogonality as necessary but insufficient and acknowledging the text–image modality gap. Appendix K adds the interpretation that larger tau makes its counterexample less problematic for approximate sampling.

D1.justification: Appendix D supplies CLIP prompts, image-filtering instructions, retained image counts, and background and averaging procedures. Appendix B.1 explicitly clarifies that existing CLEVR experiments condition on only location or color at a time. Existing architecture, hardware, training, and sampler details are preserved.

R1.justification: Adds references connecting the work to disentangled representations, CLIP, and its modality gap, including Chen et al., Kim and Mnih, Radford et al., and Liang et al. The main research positioning remains intact. Anonymous (2024) and Zhang et al. (2025) identify the same illumination-harmonization work.

P1.justification: Section 8 becomes Practical implications and separates prior-work connections from the new heuristic. The former Appendix J argument is reorganized into explicitly named intermediate results in Appendix K. Explanations and references are refined, while most existing prose and the main narrative order remain intact.

P2.justification: Adds Figure 8's paired CLIP heatmaps and Table 1, and expands Figure 6's caption. All original figure images are retained; several displays move through page reflow, including the supplementary CLEVR sample grid.

improvement.justification: Correcting the malformed mixture weights in v1 Appendix J and restructuring the argument in v2 Appendix K improves precision and auditability. Lemma 8.1 also gives the practical diagnostic an explicit, qualified basis. These gains are limited by the preliminary CLIP evidence and Table 1's inconsistent Single-object Bayes totals of 109 and 43 despite the stated 100 samples, which weaken the added quantitative validation.
